title: US FDA Puts Hyderabad Firm's Fish Masala on Salmonella Import Alert List
excerpt: Fish Masala from Tejas Food Industries LLP can now be detained at the US border without physical examination under Import Alert 99-19; the listing names no specific batch or lab result.
body:
• The US Food and Drug Administration has placed Fish Masala made by Hyderabad-based Tejas Food Industries LLP on its Salmonella import-alert Red List, allowing US officials to detain shipments at the border without physically examining them.
  • The FDA published the company-product entries in August and September 2026 under Import Alert 99-19, which governs detention without physical examination of food products linked to Salmonella.
  • The listing applies specifically to Fish Masala — not to all Tejas products — and the public entries name no batch number, shipment, US importer, or positive laboratory result from a particular consignment.
  • For readers: the action is US-border-specific and does not cover the same brand sold within India. A detained shipment can enter the US only after the importer provides evidence — such as private laboratory testing — that the product is Salmonella-free.

The US Food and Drug Administration has placed Fish Masala manufactured by Hyderabad-based Tejas Food Industries LLP on its Salmonella import-alert Red List, a move that lets American border officials detain shipments of the spice mix without inspecting them first.

The FDA published the company-product entries in August and September 2026 under Import Alert 99-19, the agency's standing system for detention without physical examination of food products linked to Salmonella, as reported by the Times of India.

Context & Background

The import alert does not accuse every product from the company. The listing covers only Fish Masala, classified by the FDA under "Spices and Seasoning, Ground/Cracked, With Salt, N.E.C." The public entries name two Tejas addresses — one in Raghavendra Colony, Kondapur, Hyderabad, and another at the TIF MSME Green Industrial Park, IP Dandu Malkapur, Choutuppal, Telangana.

Under the alert system, FDA field offices can hold listed products at the port of entry without first sampling each shipment. For a detained consignment, the US importer or another responsible party must produce evidence that the product does not contain Salmonella; private laboratory testing of a representative sample may form part of that evidence, and the FDA can also collect its own samples before deciding whether to release the shipment.

Tejas is not new to the FDA's alert lists. The company also appears in the older Import Alert 23-14, which covers detention without physical examination of foods linked to mycotoxins, including aflatoxins. That entry names the Kondapur address and lists Masala Peanut (South Indian Fried Snacks) as the product concerned. On its website, Tejas describes its unit as a "USFDA Compliant Facility" and says it exports to more than 33 countries.

Impact & Analysis

Indian spice exporters have faced recurring American regulatory scrutiny. Import alerts are firm-specific and hazard-specific: once a company-product combination appears, every future shipment faces detention unless the importer can demonstrate compliance, which typically means systematic third-party testing and documented corrective action at the plant.

The same day brought a separate Indian food-safety headline. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India said on Saturday that a sample of Nestle India's "low-fat dairy whitener," drawn from the premises of Hotel Lalit in Connaught Place, New Delhi, had been found "unsafe and substandard" by a food analyst's laboratory — a finding of non-compliance under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The regulator issued a notice to Bharat Hotels Ltd and directed it to immediately stop selling the identified product, while giving the food business operator the prescribed window to appeal.

Together, the two developments put Indian food manufacturing under a dual lens: American border enforcement on one side, domestic laboratory surveillance on the other.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian-American shoppers, the alert is narrow but worth knowing: it targets one product from one Hyderabad firm at the US border, not the spice aisle at large. Consumers who already have Tejas Fish Masala in their pantry bought from a US Indian grocery store should check the brand and product name; the FDA alert does not itself announce a retail recall.

What's Next

Tejas can petition the FDA for removal from the alert list, a process that requires demonstrating that the conditions leading to the listing have been corrected — typically through inspection evidence, corrective-action documentation, and a record of clean shipments. Until then, each US-bound consignment of its Fish Masala faces detention on arrival.
